paragraphs: The third ingredient in the vigor of the executive authority is adequate provision for its support. Without proper attention to this matter, it is clear, the separation of the executive from the legislative department would be merely nominal and worthless. If the legislature had discretionary power over the salary and pay of the chief executive, it could make him as submissive to its will as it chose. In most cases it could either starve him into compliance or tempt him with gifts, and so make him hand over his judgment to its inclinations whenever it liked. Taken in the full breadth of their terms, these expressions would no doubt say more than I intend. There are men who could be neither distressed nor won into sacrificing their duty. But this stern virtue grows in few soils, and on the whole it will be found that power over a man's support is power over his will. If so plain a truth needed confirming with facts, examples would not be lacking, even in this country, of an Executive intimidated or seduced by the threats or the enticements of the legislative body's money arrangements.

It is hard, therefore, to praise too highly the sound attention this subject has received in the proposed Constitution. It provides there that "The President of the United States shall, at stated times, receive for his services a compensation which shall neither be increased nor diminished during the period for which he shall have been elected; and he shall not receive within that period any other emolument from the United States, or any of them." No provision could be imagined that would be more desirable. When a President is appointed, the legislature is to declare once and for all what his compensation will be for the term of his election. After that, it will have no power to change it, up or down, until a new term begins with a new election. It can neither weaken his firmness by working on his needs nor corrupt his integrity by appealing to his greed. Neither the Union nor any of its members will be free to give, and he will not be free to receive, any pay other than what the first act determined. He can therefore have no money motive to give up or abandon the independence the Constitution intends for him.
The last of the requisites to energy that were listed is adequate powers. Let us now consider the ones proposed to be vested in the President of the United States.

The first thing to claim our attention is the President's qualified negative on the acts or resolutions of the two houses of the legislature. Put another way, he has the power to return any bill with his objections, and this prevents it from becoming law unless two thirds of the members of each house afterward approve it.

I have already suggested, and repeated, that the legislative department tends to intrude on the rights of the other departments and to absorb their powers. I have also remarked that a mere description of each one's boundaries on parchment is not enough, and I have concluded and proved that each must be given constitutional arms for its own defense. From these clear and undeniable principles it follows that the Executive should have a negative, whether absolute or qualified, on the acts of the legislative branches. Without one or the other, the Executive would be utterly unable to defend himself against the legislature's plundering. Resolution by resolution he might gradually be stripped of his authorities, or he might be wiped out by a single vote. Either way, the legislative and executive powers might soon come to be blended in the same hands. And even if the legislative body had never shown the slightest tendency to invade the rights of the Executive, sound reasoning and theoretical propriety would still teach us that the one ought not to be left at the mercy of the other, but ought to have a constitutional and effective power of self-defense.

But the power in question has a further use. It is not only a shield for the Executive; it is also an additional security against the passing of improper laws. It sets up a beneficial check on the legislative body, meant to protect the community from the effects of faction, of haste, or of any impulse hostile to the public good that may happen to sway a majority of that body.

Some have opposed a negative with the remark that we cannot presume a single man to have more virtue and wisdom than a number of men, and that unless we presume this, it would be improper to give the chief executive any kind of control over the legislative body.

But on examination this remark will prove more specious than solid. The propriety of the negative does not rest on supposing the Executive to have superior wisdom or virtue. It rests on supposing that the legislature will not be infallible: that its love of power may sometimes betray it into a disposition to encroach on the rights of other parts of the government; that a spirit of faction may sometimes distort its deliberations; and that the impressions of the moment may sometimes rush it into measures that it would itself condemn on calmer reflection. The primary reason for giving the Executive this power is to enable him to defend himself. The secondary reason is to improve the community's chances against the passing of bad laws, whether through haste, carelessness, or design. The more often a measure is brought up for examination, and the more varied the situations of those who examine it, the smaller must be the danger of errors that come from a lack of proper deliberation, or of missteps that come from the contagion of some shared passion or interest. It is far less probable that blameworthy views of any kind would infect every part of the government at the same moment and on the same object than that they would take control of each part in turn and mislead it.

Perhaps it will be said that the power of preventing bad laws includes that of preventing good ones, and may be used for the one purpose as readily as for the other. But this objection will carry little weight with those who can properly judge the harms of that inconstancy and instability in the laws which are the greatest blemish on the character and spirit of our governments. They will regard any institution meant to restrain excessive law-making, and to keep things in whatever state they happen to be in at a given time, as far more likely to do good than harm, because it favors greater stability in the system of legislation. The damage that may possibly be done by defeating a few good laws will be more than made up by the advantage of blocking a number of bad ones.

Nor is this all. In a free government the legislative body has superior weight and influence, and the Executive risks much in a trial of strength with it. This gives satisfactory security that the negative would generally be used with great caution, and that there would more often be grounds to charge the Executive with timidity than with rashness in using it. Even a king of Great Britain, with all his train of sovereign attributes and all the influence he draws from a thousand sources, would today hesitate to put a negative on the joint resolutions of the two houses of Parliament. He would not fail to use the utmost resources of that influence to smother a measure he disliked on its way to the throne, so as to avoid the dilemma of either letting it take effect or risking the nation's displeasure by opposing the sense of the legislative body. Nor is it likely that he would in the end venture to use his prerogatives except in a case of manifest propriety or extreme necessity. All well-informed men in that kingdom will grant that this remark is just. A very long time has passed since the crown last exercised its negative.

If an official as powerful and as well fortified as a British monarch would have scruples about using the power under consideration, how much greater caution can reasonably be expected from a President of the United States, who is clothed with the executive authority for only four years, in a government wholly and purely republican?

Plainly, there would be greater danger that he would fail to use his power when necessary than that he would use it too often or too much. An argument against its expediency has indeed been drawn from this very point. On this ground it has been called a power that is odious in appearance and useless in practice. But it does not follow that because it might rarely be used, it would never be used. In the case it is chiefly designed for, an immediate attack on the constitutional rights of the Executive, or a case in which the public good was clearly and plainly being sacrificed, a man of reasonable firmness would use his constitutional means of defense and would heed the warnings of duty and responsibility. In the first case, his firmness would be spurred by his direct interest in the power of his office. In the second, it would be spurred by the likelihood that his constituents would approve. In a doubtful case they would naturally lean toward the legislative body, but they would hardly let their bias deceive them in a very plain one. I am speaking now with a chief executive in view who has only an ordinary share of firmness. There are men who, in any circumstances, will have the courage to do their duty whatever the risk.

But the Convention has taken a middle course in this business. It will make it easier for the chief executive to use the power vested in him here, and it makes the power's effectiveness depend on the view of a considerable part of the legislative body. In place of an absolute negative, it proposes to give the Executive the qualified negative already described. This power would be much more readily used than the other. A man who might be afraid to defeat a law by his single VETO might not hesitate to return it for reconsideration, knowing that it can be finally rejected only if more than one third of each house agree that his objections were sufficient. He would be encouraged by the thought that if his opposition should prevail, a very respectable share of the legislative body would be in it with him, and their influence would join his in defending the propriety of his conduct before public opinion. A direct and categorical negative looks harsher, and is more likely to irritate, than the mere offering of reasoned objections to be approved or rejected by those they are addressed to. To the degree that it would give less offense, it would be more likely to be used, and for that very reason it may be found in practice to be more effective. It is to be hoped that improper views will seldom control as many as two thirds of both branches of the legislature at once, and this despite the counterweight of the Executive. It is in any case far less probable that this would happen than that such views would taint the resolutions and conduct of a bare majority. A power of this kind in the Executive will often work silently and unnoticed, though forcefully. When men engaged in unjustifiable pursuits know that an obstruction may come from a quarter they cannot control, the mere fear of opposition will often restrain them from doing what they would eagerly rush into if no such outside obstacles were to be feared.

As I have remarked elsewhere, this qualified negative is, in this State, vested in a council made up of the governor, the chancellor, and the judges of the Supreme Court, or any two of them. It has been freely used on a variety of occasions, and often with success. Its usefulness has become so apparent that persons who fiercely opposed it when the Constitution was being drawn up have, through experience, become its avowed admirers.(1)

I have remarked in another place that in shaping this part of its plan the Convention departed from the model of this State's constitution and followed that of Massachusetts instead. Two strong reasons for this preference can be imagined. One is that the judges, who are to be the interpreters of the law, might pick up an improper bias from having already given an opinion in their revisionary capacities. The other is that, through frequent association with the Executive, they might be led too far into the political views of that chief executive, and so a dangerous combination might gradually be cemented between the executive and judiciary departments. The judges cannot be kept too separate from every occupation but that of expounding the laws. It is especially dangerous to put them in a position where the Executive could corrupt or influence them.
1. Mr. Abraham Yates, a warm opponent of the plan of the Convention, is one of these.
